What is a Japanese Painting?

A Japanese painting is a work of art rooted in centuries of East Asian artistic tradition, most commonly created using ink and brush on paper or silk. The most iconic style is sumi-e, or ink-wash painting, where black ink is diluted to create a full range of tones from deep black to the softest misty grey — capturing landscapes, trees, mountains and water with expressive, minimal brushwork. The philosophy behind Japanese painting is closely tied to wabi-sabi and zen thinking: the beauty of simplicity, impermanence and quiet contemplation. Today, Japanese painting-inspired wall art prints bring that same calm, meditative energy into modern homes and offices, particularly in Japandi-style interiors that value natural tones, clean lines and meaningful simplicity.

1. Plan your wall space: Measure the wall area you have available and lay the three prints out on the floor first to check the overall width. Aim for a combined display that is roughly two-thirds the width of any furniture beneath it — this keeps everything visually balanced.

2. Find your eye level: The centre of the artwork should sit at roughly 145–150 cm from the floor — this is the standard gallery hanging height and feels natural whether you are sitting at a desk or standing in the room.

3. Space the panels evenly: Keep the gap between each of the three prints consistent — 3 to 5 cm is ideal. Mark your fixing points lightly in pencil before you commit, and use a spirit level to keep the row perfectly straight.

4. Step back and adjust: Once all three are up, step back to the opposite side of the room and check the alignment. The landscape should read as one flowing scene from left to right — if a panel looks slightly off, adjust it before the hooks settle.

5. Style around it: Keep surrounding decor simple. A low desk plant, a neutral ceramic or a single dried stem nearby complements the zen, Japandi mood without competing with the artwork.
